articles.title: Kelsey Grammer still feels 'sense of smallness' for not serving in military: 'I do my best to make up for it'
articles.excerpt:
The actor admitted to feeling "an annoying sense of smallness" for having never served in the military, but says he does what he can to "make up for it."

Kelsey Grammer feels he missed an opportunity...
articles.body_text:
The actor admitted to feeling "an annoying sense of smallness" for having never served in the military, but says he does what he can to "make up for it."

Kelsey Grammer feels he missed an opportunity to give back to his country by not serving in the military when he was younger.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 71-year-old actor discussed his latest project, "America the Beautiful," a 40-minute giant screen documentary, and why he always does his best to "show up for the military" when he is able to.

"I will always have an annoying sort of sense of smallness that I didn't serve, but I do my best to make up for it," he said.

He explained that despite feeling that way, he is unsure if he would have made a different decision if given the opportunity to do his life over again, noting, "It was a really interesting time."

Grammer admits to feeling "a sense of smallness" because he never served in the military. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images)

HOLLYWOOD MARINE VETERAN ROB RIGGLE DOUBTS MODERN STARS WOULD MAKE JIMMY STEWART'S WWII SACRIFICE

WATCH: Kelsey Grammer feels a ‘sense of smallness’ for not having served in the military

When he was a young man, he said that the Vietnam War was "sort of in full flair," and that he had signed up for the draft and was ready to go fight had his number been drawn, but said, "President Nixon pulled us out just before I would have gone down to get my number."

"So I was thankful for not having to go, make that decision, but I would've gone. If my number had been up, I woulda gone. But I was, I was thankful not to," he said. "I used to work in San Diego, it was one of my first jobs at the Shakespeare Festival there, and I would go over to the Point Loma Military Graveyard and have a lunch sometimes, and I'd sit next to this cross that I'd found of a young man who was really only eight months older than I was, who had died in Vietnam. And it just broke my heart."

Grammer said he used to eat lunch at a military cemetery when working at the Shakespeare Festival. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

As a father, Grammer says he speaks to his children about the many sacrifices people have made to ensure the safety of America, adding that he "will always try and instruct them with the idea that service to your country is a good idea."

KELSEY GRAMMER WARNS OF CHILLING DANGER FACING AMERICANS WHO FORGET NATION'S FOUNDING HISTORY

WATCH: Kelsey Grammer’s grandfather was an ‘inspiration’ to him

He says that together they discuss the Revolutionary War and all the great battles throughout history, noting he would encourage them to serve their country if they wanted, but said that "their mom would get mad at me." He noted however, that this is something "people have been doing" for many years.

Grammer said he would support his sons wanting to join the military. (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

"There's a lot of wonderful patriotic people in our country today whose children and whose husbands and wives are serving, and my hat is off to them all. And we salute them. I mean, with this particular thing, the 11 hour, the 11 day, 11th month, Armistice Day originally, now Veterans Day at the end of the First World War. Remarkable. The number of people who died in that war," he said. "So certainly the hope was that it would never happen again and sure enough, a generation later, we were fighting World War II. Amazing. And we go on. We continue. Hopefully it'll end one day."

Grammer feels a strong connection to Veterans Day, as his grandfather served as a Colonel in the Army Corps of Engineers during World War II. When speaking about his grandfather, the "Frasier" star said he "was always an inspiration to me."

Grammer said his grandfather inspired him when he was younger. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)

"I looked up to him like a kid would," he said. "I mean he raised me, but his bravery and his courage and his commitment to the country, these were active, living, breathing things that he was … he embodied that. And so, it's always been my hope to kind of pass that along a little bit. At least a remembrance of him, respect for what he was able to do in the face of extraordinary hardship."

CARRIE UNDERWOOD, GARY SINISE LEAD STARS WHO'VE SHARED WHY THEY'RE PROUD TO BE AMERICANS

One way in which Grammer is honoring his grandfather, and all the other men and women who have served the country, is through his new film, "America the Beautiful," which is set to hit screens on Nov. 11.

Grammer is honoring veterans with his new film, "America the Beautiful." (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The film was created in honor of America's 250th birthday, and celebrates the beauty of the country and the love of the land Americans share for it.

WATCH: Kelsey Grammer’s new documentary, ‘America the Beautiful’ showcases the beauty of the country

"That was the original idea of the movie, why they made it, and they invited me to join in. I think it's absolutely apropos. I mean, without the sacrifices that have been made by our military men and women, then we might not actually have this treasure of national beauty that we do have," he said. "The Americans that have gotten to know our national forests and our national parks. They are inspired by them every day and blessed by the fact that they're still here. And I think that speaks in large part of the sacrifices that people make abroad and at home to secure our future and to defend our country."

Through making the film, he was able to understand President Theodore Roosevelt's philosophy that "we have to preserve our physical life as well as our creative and our ideological life." He learned how Roosevelt was allotted "time to seek solace in nature" and gather inspiration and comfort from it, leading him to create the national park system believing "everybody should be able to have" the same "personal relationship with the wilderness" as he found.

Grammer's hope for the film is that audiences are able to understand the "overwhelming beauty we have been given" in this country, calling it "powerful" and saying "it defines us."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Grammer hopes audiences are overwhelmed with the beauty of America after watching his new film. (Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Paramount+)

Of all the places he visited, he called the Badlands his favorite, saying "I felt like I was in a holy place" while he was there, saying it felt like being "in God's land."

"It was just an amazing day we spent there and, of course, then we went and saw the Mount Rushmore. We also saw on the way there 's's a mountain called a crazy horse which is like four times bigger than Mount Rushmore," he said. "It's an amazing thing that a private family's been working on it for 60 years, maybe longer, where it's just crazy horse seated on his steed, and he says, with his finger pointing outwards, sort of like this, he says my lands are where my dead lie buried."

WATCH: Kelsey Grammer hopes viewers see ‘the overwhelming beauty we have been given’ in new documentary

He continued: "And that's powerful stuff, but I think that is an American saying. That is an American occurrence. It's these two cultures clashed, and then he became a new culture together, but it's all based on that land, this extraordinary land that we have. And yeah, it's a rainbow. It's a cornucopia of life and teaming, teaming life, renewal, power, all these things that actually really are America. They live here, and I'm proud to have done the movie."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"America the Beautiful" premieres on Wednesday, Nov. 11, and will be available on IMAX, Giant Screen and dome theaters. (Mathew Tsang/Getty Images)

"America the Beautiful" premieres on Wednesday, Nov. 11, and will be available on IMAX, Giant Screen and Dome theaters, with some theaters offering free screenings for veterans on Veterans Day.

Visit americathebeautifulmovie.com for a list of where to find the film.

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Veteran actor Irma P Hall, star of The Ladykillers, dies aged 91
articles.excerpt:
Once a Dallas school teacher, Hall became a star in later life with roles in Soul Food and Collateral

Actor Irma P Hall, star of Soul Food and the Coen brothers’ The Ladykillers, has died at the age ...
articles.body_text:
Once a Dallas school teacher, Hall became a star in later life with roles in Soul Food and Collateral

Actor Irma P Hall, star of Soul Food and the Coen brothers’ The Ladykillers, has died at the age of 91.

Hall died on Tuesday, her family confirmed alongside a statement that described her as “a beloved actress, author, poet, educator and public speaker whose contributions touched countless lives throughout her remarkable career”.

In an acting career that spanned six decades, Hall starred opposite Denzel Washington, Oprah Winfrey, Robin Williams and Tom Hanks, and worked with directors including Michael Mann, the Coen brothers and Jonathan Demme.

Born in Texas in 1935, Hall was raised with a passion for the arts as the daughter of saxophone player Samuel Player. For 27 years she worked as a high school teacher in Houston before pivoting to acting the early 1980s.

“I always believed I could do whatever I wanted,” she said in a 2001 interview. “I never knew there [were things] I wasn’t supposed to be able to do because I was Black or a woman.”

After roles in 1980s films including On Valentine’s Day and They Still Call Me Bruce, Hall starred alongside Hollywood A-listers such as Dolly Parton in Straight Talk and John Goodman in The Babe, before her career progressed to the next level in the mid-90s.

In the 1997 drama Soul Food, she played Big Mama Joseph, the unforgiving matriarch to three daughters (Vanessa Williams, Vivica A Fox and Nia Long). Hall won the outstanding supporting actress award at the NAACP Image awards for her portrayal. She resumed the role of Big Mama in a TV spin-off of the film which aired from 2000-2004.

She also worked with Robin Williams in 90s comedy drama Patch Adams and Clint Eastwood in the fact-based crime drama Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil.

In 2004, Hall received a Cannes special jury prize for her work in the Coen brothers’ The Ladykillers, in which she played spiky landlady Marva Munson. The same year, she played the no-nonsense mother of Jamie Foxx’s character in Mann’s thriller Collateral.

Hall’s later films include Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans; My Son, My Son, What Have Ye Done and the Sundance TV show Hap and Leonard.

The actor consistently advocated for the arts community and helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre. Since 2015, the Irma P Hall Black Theatre awards have been annually held to recognize artistic achievement in the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

For many years, Hall was church mother at Dallas’s Inspiring Body of Christ church and a treasured member of the local religious community.

“Our beloved Church Mother, Irma P Hall, has taken her final bow on the stage of life and stepped into eternity,” said pastor Rickie G Rush in a statement. “While we mourn her passing, we are forever grateful for the remarkable legacy she leaves behind.”

“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said. “My mom used to always say, ‘To the world you may be one person, but to one person you may be the world.’ And she was just that to many people.”

articles.title: Former ESPN star Sean Salisbury says political arguments wore out fans who just wanted sports
articles.excerpt: Former ESPN analyst Sean Salisbury told OutKick that political debates and the chase for social media clicks wore on viewers, pointing to "College GameDay" as a sign the network may be getting back on...
articles.body_text:
Former ESPN analyst Sean Salisbury told OutKick that political debates and the chase for social media clicks wore on viewers, pointing to "College GameDay" as a sign the network may be getting back on track.

Sean Salisbury thinks ESPN lost sight of the person coming home after a long day at work who just wanted to watch some sports. That viewer wanted highlights and a few laughs. Instead, Salisbury said, too much of the programming became another argument about politics.

"If I want that, I'll get it on a different channel," he told OutKick.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

I spoke with the former NFL quarterback and ESPN analyst in October about the network where we both worked. Salisbury spent 12 years there, leaving in 2008. I arrived in 2012 and stayed until 2021.

ESPN’S FAVORITE INSIDER ACCIDENTALLY EXPLAINED WHY MOST AMERICANS DON’T TRUST THE MEDIA

To me, ESPN was at its best in the early 2000s. Salisbury was part of that, along with the people who made you want to watch a studio show even when you already knew what happened in the games.

"It was sports first with entertainment personalities," Salisbury said.

Former NFL quarterback Sean Salisbury, pictured in 2015, told OutKick that ESPN lost its way when it leaned into politics over sports. (Getty Images)

He remembered watching the same edition of SportsCenter several times because he enjoyed the people delivering the highlights.

Salisbury's father was a blue-collar worker, and that shaped how he thought about the people watching him on television. Someone who had spent all day working construction probably wanted to sit down and enjoy a game or some highlights.

Salisbury believes ESPN made that harder by letting political and social arguments take up too much of its programming.

"We really weren't concerned with what the color of the skin of the quarterback was because we were just talking football," he said of his years at the network.

He also blamed the pressure to generate a reaction on social media. In his view, talking about the sports news increasingly gave way to trying to become the sports news, with arguments designed to get people sharing clips.

CNN PANELIST BLAMES 'CULTURE WAR' RETRIBUTION AS REASON FOR RYAN CLARK'S ESPN DEPARTURE

I think that's a big part of it. Once getting a reaction becomes the goal, there's always a reason to make the next argument more outlandish and controversial. Eventually, the viewer who wanted to hear about his team has to sit through a debate about something an analyst said on another show.

Salisbury acknowledged that politics and sports overlap, and he said those subjects deserve coverage when they're relevant. His complaint was about how much of the programming those discussions consumed.

"That should be the outlier, not the every single day grind," he said.

Our conversation started with the argument over Emmanuel Acho's comments about NFL Live. In July, Acho credited Ryan Clark with building the show into a "juggernaut." He acknowledged that Clark hadn't created it, but dismissed its earlier audience by claiming "nobody was watching NFL Live then."

Earlier this year, ESPN parted ways with longtime NFL analyst Ryan Clark, a commentator who frequently fixated on race and left-wing politics. (Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

As I pointed out on social media, that's false. NFL Live averaged around 650,000 daily viewers in 2011 and 2012, before Clark was even hired by ESPN. The version featuring Clark never averaged an audience that size.

Salisbury and former host Trey Wingo both weighed in on social media, as well. Wingo wrote, "'Let your apology be as loud as your disrespect.' I think somebody said that once."

Salisbury posted, "Should one of us tell him" and tagged NFL Live alums Wingo, Mark Schlereth, Mike Golic, Merril Hoge, and Mark Malone.

"Acho was about two decades late to the party on that one, so no shock there," he told me.

He compared overlooking the original group to talking about Led Zeppelin without Jimmy Page. Other people could come along and do good work, but that didn't erase what the earlier crew had built.

And Salisbury's memories of that period went well beyond wanting credit for NFL Live. He talked about learning from broadcasters whose personalities made the shows worth watching, particularly Dan Patrick, Chris Berman and Mike Tirico.

That's the ESPN he wants people to be able to turn on again.

When I got hired at ESPN in 2012, the reaction from my family was pretty much what you'd expect: "You got a job at ESPN? That's incredible!"

By the time I left in 2021, some of those same people had a very different reaction to hearing where I worked. "You work at ESPN? Oh."

I told Salisbury that I don't miss working at ESPN. But I do miss producing live radio.

I'd spend all week preparing a four-hour Saturday show, then news would break while we were on the air and we'd have to adjust. I loved that part of the job. There were a lot of moving pieces, and getting it right gave me an adrenaline rush.

PAUL FINEBAUM SAYS ESPN BANNED HIM FROM SHOWS AFTER TELLING OUTKICK HE MIGHT RUN FOR OFFICE

Salisbury knew exactly what I meant. For him, live television was about as close as broadcasting could get to the feeling of playing quarterback in the NFL.

He recalled sitting beside Tirico on Monday Night Countdown when a camera went down just before the show started. Salisbury was sweating over how they were going to handle it. Tirico made it look routine.

"Nobody at home would have ever known," Salisbury said.

Former ESPN analyst Sean Salisbury spoke glowingly about his time working with Mike Tirico. (Perry Knotts/Getty Images)

He also repeatedly credited the producers and other employees behind the scenes who made those shows work. His years at ESPN gave him close friends and taught him how to do the broadcasting work he still does.

"Those 12 years changed my life," he said.

Salisbury still sees programming at ESPN that delivers what he's talking about. He singled out College GameDay, calling it "the best studio show on the planet."

Salisbury wants ESPN's analysts saying what they actually believe.

"I think sometimes we all get caught up in it, saying stuff to appease somebody else as opposed to what you actually believe, and I'm just not willing to do that," Salisbury said. "I think it loses credibility."

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The ESPN Salisbury and I remember gave viewers a reason to keep watching after the highlights were over. He thinks the network still has the people to do that, provided it remembers why those viewers turned on a sports channel in the first place.

"Hopefully we can get back to where we're actually talking sports more than we're talking about why somebody should have voted for somebody else," he said.

articles.title: Which key races remain undecided one week after the US midterms?
articles.excerpt:
It has been more than a week since voters in the United States cast ballots in the midterm elections.

But the size of Democrats’ majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate remained undeter...
articles.body_text:
It has been more than a week since voters in the United States cast ballots in the midterm elections.

But the size of Democrats’ majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate remained undetermined. More than a dozen congressional races are still waiting to be called.

Democrats have already won 54 Senate seats in the incoming Congress in January, but they could pick up one or two more as votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi.

Meanwhile, in the House of Representatives, Democrats have notched their largest elected majority since 2008, with 255 seats in the 435-member chamber. But they have the potential to add to their lead with several more seats as the remaining races are decided.

Here’s a look at where things stand in some of the uncalled races:

Late on Tuesday, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for the US Senate in Mississippi.

There are two key deadlines in the vote-counting process in Mississippi this week: Mail-in absentee ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday.

It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.

Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, journalists from The Associated Press and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.

The state will certify its results on December 3.

On Monday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said about 14,200 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80 percent were accepted, and about 2,700 mail-in absentee ballots had not yet been returned.

Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The Associated Press may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes in Alaska’s US Senate race as of Tuesday, with an estimated 76 percent of the vote counted.

Absentee ballots are among those that continue to be counted. The final absentee ballots mailed from outside the US are accepted as late as November 18, which is 15 days after Election Day.

Ranked-choice voting could also affect the timeline. Peltola is just over one percentage point short of the majority needed to win outright. If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked-choice tabulation on November 18.

The state’s “target date” for certifying the election results is November 25.

Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state’s certification.

In most of the US House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than one percentage point among votes counted, as of late Tuesday afternoon.

In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in each one. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is one percent or less of the total votes.

The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on November 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results on November 24.

In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber’s balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail-in ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties must certify their results by December 3. The state will certify its results on December 11.

In South Carolina’s 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalifa. Wilson led Khalifa by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99 percent of the votes had been counted.

In Minnesota’s 1st District, the race was still undecided late by Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99 percent of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25 percent of the vote.

In Tennessee’s 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of Tuesday. In that state, recounts are held only as part of a legal challenge in the courts. There are no automatic recounts, and losing candidates may not request recounts.

In the race to be Kansas’s next governor, Democratic state Senator Cindy Holscher led state Republican Senate President Ty Masterson by less than one percentage point on Tuesday.

On November 4, the state announced that a close-race audit had been triggered in six close Kansas races, including the gubernatorial race.

That process requires a hand count of selected ballots, and it must be completed before November 16, the day by which counties must certify their results.

In the race for governor of Alaska, only about 76 percent of votes were estimated to have been counted by Tuesday.

The Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Jonathan Kreiss‑Tomkins, was leading Bernadette Wilson by about 45,000 votes, 49.6 percent to 28.9 percent. The race will advance to ranked-choice tabulation if no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote.

articles.title: Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say
articles.excerpt:
Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court

MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer whe...
articles.body_text:
Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court

MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal.

The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning.

The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.

The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought.

Directors of Poundland are now seeking a further 10 working days’ grace, which must be approved by the high court. That comes after Gordon Brothers, which is understood to be supportive of the extension, released £10m more in funds to help Poundland secure new stock and keep trading.

Without the legal protection in place, Poundland is likely to have to call in administrators; the advisory firm Alix Partners is already lined up.

The European head of Gordon Brothers, Mark Newton-Jones, gave evidence in private for almost two hours to the Commons business select committee on Wednesday afternoon after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee, said that after questioning Newton-Jones he was “deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers’ behaviour may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”.
 
 
 He said: “Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a ‘knife-edge’.
 
 
 “Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there’s concerning signs it’s been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run-up to Christmas.
 
 
 “Worse, Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.”

The committee separately heard from Poundland’s management team, led by Barry Williams, who had been fighting to save the business.

Sources said Poundland continued to trade well, with sales up year on year, despite its problems, but it has only enough cash to support the business for a short period. Gordon Brothers has said Poundland remains “challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading”.

Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with three potential bidders for the entire chain but has indicated it can raise more from a break-up of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers.

The bids are understood to be worth less than the £30m in debts taken on by shareholders when Gordon Brothers bought the chain. It bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.

Pepco still holds £7.5m of the £30m shareholder debt. It is prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.

Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group, the Northern Irish family-owned firm supporting a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which includes the Dealz chain in Ireland.

Martin Property Group’s first bid had been rejected by Gordon Brothers as it amounted to no more than half the £30m it wants for Poundland with less than £7m up front.

A little-known finance company, Xyra Group, is thought to have offered about £12m up front and close to £30m in total. However, Xyra has not been involved with retail businesses previously.

Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Double amputee marathon runner criticises Badenoch for ‘weaponising his success’
articles.excerpt:
Paralympian Richard Whitehead ‘gobsmacked’ at Tory leader’s speech over proposed £36bn welfare cuts

The double amputee marathon runner Richard Whitehead has criticised Kemi Badenoch for “weaponising ...
articles.body_text:
Paralympian Richard Whitehead ‘gobsmacked’ at Tory leader’s speech over proposed £36bn welfare cuts

The double amputee marathon runner Richard Whitehead has criticised Kemi Badenoch for “weaponising his sporting success” to justify her proposed £36bn welfare cuts.

The Conservative leader used the example of “double amputees running marathons” in a speech this week to explain the reasoning behind her proposed cuts to disability benefits, which she said were enabling people to “live a life of dependency”.

Whitehead said he had been surprised at her comments and angry that his achievements were being used as part of a campaign to take money “from the most vulnerable that actually need it”.

“I was gobsmacked that somebody’s sporting success would be weaponised in this way,” he said. “To say everybody should work because double-leg amputees run marathons, I was like, wow. It’s very divisive language.

“I understand the welfare system needs a shake-up, but you shouldn’t be blanket taking money away from individuals who need it, it’s their lifeline. There are families out there relying on the support.”

Whitehead has run more than 100 marathons, set world records and won four Paralympic medals over the course of his career, while also completing endurance feats to raise money for charity.

He said several people had sent him clips of Badenoch’s speech on Tuesday and “his mouth was open” as he watched it.

After saying there were “people who genuinely cannot work”, Badenoch went on to say: “The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities, even when they face serious challenges.

“Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.”

Whitehead immediately expressed his concerns about the comments on social media. “Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day,” he wrote.

“One person’s ability to overcome significant challenges should never be used to justify withdrawing support from others.”

He invited Badenoch to have a conversation with him to learn more about disability and how it had affected his life and how he used his platform to inspire and mentor others.

“She’s utilising somebody’s success and 50 years of hard work for her own means without actually having any knowledge of who I am and the work that I do,” he said. “When I stand on a podium, I use that moment to hopefully inspire and liberate people of all minorities. She’s just looked for a headline.

“I think she needs to really reflect and think about how she communicates with the disabled community, and maybe have a conversation with myself around the work that I’m doing.”

The Conservatives said welfare savings would be made by ending disability living allowance payments to families of children with “milder cases” of behavioural disorders, learning disabilities or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Badenoch said in her speech: “If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself.”

Whitehead said: “I would like a response from her on the terminology she used and I could educate her about the real scenario for people with neurodiversity, with ADHD, who are really struggling. And maybe with that experience she will understand that maybe she’s got it wrong.”

articles.title: British soldier charged with rape of army servicewoman in Cyprus
articles.excerpt:
L/Cpl Nicholas Horne, from 4th Battalion of Royal Regiment of Scotland, charged with one count of rape on 23 October

A British soldier has been charged with the alleged rape of a UK army servicewoman...
articles.body_text:
L/Cpl Nicholas Horne, from 4th Battalion of Royal Regiment of Scotland, charged with one count of rape on 23 October

A British soldier has been charged with the alleged rape of a UK army servicewoman in Cyprus.

L/Cpl Nicholas Horne, who serves in the 4th Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, also known as The Highlanders, was charged with one count of rape on 23 October, the Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) said.

He was arrested on 19 October, two days after the DSCC was informed of the reported rape of a woman serving in British Forces Cyprus.

Horne was remanded in custody pending a court-martial hearing.

The charge comes after an investigation of the DSCC’s major crime team, conducted with service police partners.

A British army spokesperson said: “We can confirm that L/Cpl Nicholas Horne was charged with one count of rape on 23 October 2026, following an investigation by the Defence Serious Crime Command.

“We recognise the great courage it takes to come forward and report an offence. Anyone convicted of a sexual offence will be discharged from the service”

The DSCC, which investigates serious crime committed by military personnel, said anyone affected by sexual offences in the armed forces is encouraged to contact them.

The Ministry of Defence has stepped up efforts to tackle sexual violence and sexual misconduct in recent years.

Last year it announced specialist teams would be deployed at UK military locations in the UK and overseas. The move came after the MoD’s first official survey of sexual harassment across the armed forces found nearly one in 10 women serving full-time in the British military had been subjected to an assault or other non-consensual sexual activity in the previous year.

articles.title: Tampa Bay Lightning visit Buffalo Sabres with both goalies struggling to stop pucks this season
articles.excerpt:
Former NHL player Viktor Stalberg recounts a wild week in Russia's KHL in which he was nearly waived, traded, and then suddenly not traded by a hockey coaching great.

It has been a while since I put ...
articles.body_text:
Former NHL player Viktor Stalberg recounts a wild week in Russia's KHL in which he was nearly waived, traded, and then suddenly not traded by a hockey coaching great.

It has been a while since I put out an NHL play, and I'd like to get a bit more consistent with playing NHL games. There isn't a huge slate of games tonight, but there are certainly some intriguing ones. Hockey is the one sport that I don't follow quite as much, but I've made concerted efforts over the years to try to follow the regular season closer. It seems like this year has had more big names with trade requests (earlier) too, and has been a pretty exciting early season. Tonight, the Lightning and Sabres battle in one of the better games of the night.

The Tampa Bay Lightning are off to a great start with an 11-4-2 record. All four of their losses, though, have been on the road. They are just 3-4-2 for the season on the road. Their offense has looked great this season with a 3.71 goals-per-game average, but they are allowing 3.06 goals per game as well. Their defense probably needs to improve in terms of giving up good looks. They are allowing just 24.7 shots per game, but if they are giving up three goals per game, either the shots are good ones, or the goalie play is lacking.

Tampa Bay Lightning goaltender Andrei Vasilevskiy (88) hugs Boston Bruins right wing David Pastrnak after the Lightning defeated the Bruins during a shootout in a Stadium Series NHL hockey game Sunday, Feb. 1, 2026, in Tampa, Florida. (AP Photo/Chris O'Meara)

Over the past five games, the Lightning have won three games and lost the other two, with one in a shootout. Andrei Vasilevskiy is likely to be in the net tonight. He is 8-4-1 for the season and is allowing 2.85 goals per game, which is 24th in the nation. He only has an .883 save percentage, which puts him at 33rd in the league. As a starting goalie, that wouldn't even rank him as a top option in the league. He has been in the net for all four of the road losses this season as well.

NHL'S REIGNING MVP NIKITA KUCHEROV REPORTEDLY ASKS LIGHTNING FOR TRADE IN STUNNING MOVE

The Buffalo Sabres are not exactly great to start the season, but they aren't playing poorly either. For the season, Buffalo is 8-6-3, and only 4-5-0 for the year on their home ice. Their offense has been fine, but not great. The Sabres are scoring just under three goals per game, and they allow 3.29 goals per game. The Sabres are allowing about the same number of shots per game to opponents as they are taking. The Sabres are playing decent enough hockey lately, but they are 1-2 at home in their current home streak.

Buffalo Sabres center Tage Thompson celebrates his goal with defenseman Rasmus Dahlin during the third period against the New York Islanders in Buffalo, New York, on March 31, 2026. (Jeffrey T. Barnes/AP Photo)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Tonight, they are likely to send the owner of my favorite name in hockey, Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen, into the net. The 27-year-old Finniard hasn't been that impressive this season. Luukkonen is allowing 3.27 goals per game, which is 38th in the league. He also has an .878 save percentage this season, putting him at 48th in the league. Just like Vasilevskiy, this makes Luukkonen not even starter-level quality. He has been better at home this season than on the road. In his home games, he is only allowing 2.88 goals per game.

Tampa Bay Lightning right wing Nikita Kucherov (86) looks on against the Vegas Golden Knights in the second period at T-Mobile Arena. (Candice Ward-Imagn Images)

Neither of the defenses look that good this season, and the goalies are letting a lot of pucks past them. On offense, they are both averaging three goals. Neither has been scoring a ton in recent games, though. Tampa has gone over 6.5 goals in three of the past five games. Buffalo has had seven or more goals in a game in just two of the past five games. I do think this is one that finds at least seven goals between the two teams. Give me the over.

articles.title: Horny bull elk keeps attacking cars, forces Missouri wildlife park to close indefinitely
articles.excerpt: Country music star Chris Janson tells OutKick OutDoors about his challenging elk hunt in Colorado, where he finally harvested a bull in the final 30 minutes of his trip. The "Buy Me a Boat" singer als...
articles.body_text:
Country music star Chris Janson tells OutKick OutDoors about his challenging elk hunt in Colorado, where he finally harvested a bull in the final 30 minutes of his trip. The "Buy Me a Boat" singer also explains why he takes the sport so seriously.

A wildlife park in Missouri has been forced to close indefinitely because one particularly aggressive bull elk won't stop attacking visitors' cars.

Lone Elk Park, located just outside St. Louis, closed Monday after officials decided the animal had become too much of a safety risk. Apparently, the problem is that he's young, he's horny, and he's new to this whole being-in-charge thing.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

According to St. Louis Public Radio, the bull recently replaced his own father as the dominant male in the herd. This is his first mating season running the show, and he's not exactly handling his newfound responsibilities gracefully.

A bull elk flicks his tongue as part of the mating ritual while watching over his harem of cow elk on the Lake Estes Golf Course. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"We have a younger, more inexperienced herd bull this year," Eric Johnson, acting director of St. Louis County Parks and Recreation, said. "It's his first year, and he's acting a little bit like a teenager."

One visitor, Theresa Hammer, learned that the hard way.

Hammer told St. Louis Public Radio she was sitting in her Ford Fusion last week when the bull approached her vehicle. She looked away briefly, and when she looked back, he was ramming his antlers into the front of her car.

"I looked back up, and he hit the front of my car with his horns," she said. "He scratched up the whole side of my car, my hood and put a big dent in the rear quarter panel."

A bull elk stands in Colorado during rutting season. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Despite the damage, Hammer said she doesn't blame the elk. After all, she's the one driving through his home.

Lone Elk Park is a 546-acre drive-through wildlife park where visitors can observe elk, bison and other animals from their vehicles. Officials had posted warnings about keeping a safe distance from the elk, but visitors weren't always following them.

And with the bull becoming increasingly aggressive, the county decided it was safer to close the park until he settles down.

BULL ELK IN COLORADO NICKNAMED 'SMASH' IS CHASING OFF TRUCKS AND GOLF CARTS

For what it's worth, this kind of behavior isn't unusual during the elk rut, which is the annual breeding season. Bull elk experience a surge in testosterone and become more territorial as they compete for females. That can make them particularly dangerous to people who get too close.

But even by elk standards, this guy is apparently a handful.

Johnson, who has worked for the parks department for 32 years, said it's been roughly a decade since they've dealt with a bull quite this worked up.

"Some of [the bulls] have it figured out and they calmly go about their business, and sometimes it's like this," he said.

A bull elk wanders across Moraine Park in Rocky Mountain National Park on Wednesday, Sept. 14, 2022. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Officials haven't announced a reopening date, but they're monitoring the bull's behavior daily and hope to reopen the park within the next several days.

So, for now, an entire wildlife park is closed because one young elk can't get his hormones under control.

articles.title: Russian Ambassador to US Alexander Darchiev dies suddenly at 66
articles.excerpt:
Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on the arrest of a senior U.S. Army officer in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia following a joint U.S.-U.K. investigation.

Russia's Ambassador to the United ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on the arrest of a senior U.S. Army officer in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia following a joint U.S.-U.K. investigation.

Russia's Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev, 66, died suddenly Wednesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced.

"The leadership and staff of the Russian Foreign Ministry report with deep sorrow that on Nov. 11, at the age of 66, the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Russian Federation to the United States of America, Alexander Nikitich Darchiev, passed away suddenly," Russia's statement, as translated to English, said. "A distinguished diplomat, experienced leader, kind colleague, and mentor has departed this life. A consummate professional and brilliant Americanist, A.N. Darchiev served on one of the most critical and demanding fronts of Russian foreign policy."

"We express our deepest and most sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of Alexander Nikitich Darchiev," the statement added. "The cherished memory of our untimely departed colleague will forever remain in our hearts."

Fox News confirmed the death came in Russia and not the U.S.

MELANIA TRUMP HAILS OLESHKY CEASEFIRE AS POTENTIAL ‘SPARK’ FOR PROGRESS AMID UKRAINE-RUSSIA WAR

Alexander Darchiyev, head of the Russian Foreign Ministry's North America Department and a candidate for the position of ambassador to the United States, poses for a picture before a session of the Federation Council's committee on foreign affairs in Moscow, Russia, on Nov. 25, 2024. (Kommersant Photo/Dmitry Dukhanin via Reuters)

Russia's Vladimir Putin appointed Darchiev, a veteran diplomat known in the past for his public denunciations of the West, as ambassador to Washington in March 2025 to lead a rapprochement with the Trump administration that has rattled Ukraine, the European Union and NATO.

His death comes less than a week after a White House news conference hailing a temporary ceasefire in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia.

First lady Melania Trump and envoys from both Russia and Ukraine hailed the ceasefire in the Oleshky region.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace. Every significant transformation begins with a small spark."

KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION

Shortly after being tapped as ambassador, Darchiev met with Trump administration officials and delivered a message of hope for peace.

"Russia and the United States are destined, as great powers, to have non-confrontational peaceful existence," Darchiev said during a June 10, 2025, Russia Day reception at the Russian Embassy in Washington after delivering his credentials to the White House, adding, "our discussion was very constructive."

Before taking the helm of the Russian Embassy in Washington, Darchiev played a role as the Kremlin’s point man for high-stakes bilateral negotiations, most notably during the delicate discussions that led to prisoner swaps involving imprisoned arms dealer Viktor Bout and detained Americans Brittney Griner and Paul Whelan.

EVAN GERSHKOVICH DETAILS RUSSIAN ARREST, REVEALS MOMENT THAT NEARLY BROKE HIM DURING WRONGFUL DETENTION

In August 2022, while serving as the director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s North American Department, Darchiev provided the first on-the-record Russian confirmation that Moscow and Washington were actively discussing those situations.

"This quite sensitive issue of the swap of convicted Russian and U.S. citizens is being pursued along the channels designated by our presidents," Darchiev told the Russian state news agency TASS. "The individuals are, indeed, being discussed. The Russian side has long been seeking the release of Viktor Bout. The negotiations are bearing fruit."

An empty table for the Russian Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev is visible during a Senate Appropriations Subcommittee hearing on "The Abduction of Ukrainian Children by the Russian Federation" on Capitol Hill on December 3, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

His comments marked a breakthrough moment in months of backchannel diplomacy, which ultimately culminated in December 2022 when the U.S. and Russia completed a one-for-one swap of Griner for Bout at an airport in Abu Dhabi.

Fox News' Gillian Turner, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

articles.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
articles.excerpt:
74-year-old Leonardo Bertulazzi, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from ...
articles.body_text:
74-year-old Leonardo Bertulazzi, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.

Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.

On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.

The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks between 1969 and 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.

Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.

A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.

“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.

The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.

Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.

Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

articles.title: Teen charged with murder in fatal shooting of 15-year-old NYC student Javits Frimpong
articles.excerpt: President Donald Trump exits the stage to the parents of Jacob Freytes, a Bronx boy who was killed by a repeat criminal's stray bullet. Trump was on Long Island, N.Y., Friday addressing law enforcemen...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump exits the stage to the parents of Jacob Freytes, a Bronx boy who was killed by a repeat criminal's stray bullet. Trump was on Long Island, N.Y., Friday addressing law enforcement about his administration's crackdown on crime.

A 17-year-old boy has been arrested after a teenager was fatally shot while walking to school in New York City last month, police announced Wednesday.

The teen suspect, who has not been publicly identified, faces a murder charge in the Oct. 29 death of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong, according to the New York City Police Department (NYPD).

"The NYPD will be relentless in our efforts to get dangerous people out of our communities, especially when it involves the murder of a 15-year-old boy," the department wrote in a post on X.

Members of the community visit and maintain a memorial for Javits Frimpong Nov. 7 in the Bronx borough of New York City. Frimpong, a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana, was shot to death more than a week earlier. He was being bullied at school, and a 17-year-old boy has been arrested on suspicion of the killing. (Corbis via Getty Images)

Javits, a Ghanaian immigrant, was fatally shot in the stomach in the Bronx. His father believes the killing may be linked to ongoing bullying his son experienced at school.

Just two days before the tragedy, the school’s principal had called Thomas Frimpong to report that his son was being targeted and that two students had been suspended as a result.

The tragic killing sparked local protests and urgent calls from community members to end youth violence and bullying.

Last week, NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny noted that investigators were exploring multiple angles.

"The alleged bullying is one aspect that we’re looking at, as well as some others," Kenny told the New York Post.

"All three gave chase," Kenny added. "And these cowards shot him in the back. If their intention was to rob him, he dropped his backpack."

PARENTS IN BRONX NEIGHBORHOOD PLEAD FOR NYPD GUARD AS MAMDANI CUTS COPS, HALTS HIRES: 'HORRIBLE SITUATION'

Members of the community visit and maintain a memorial for Javits Frimpong on Nov. 7, 2026, in the Bronx borough of New York City. Frimpong, a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana, was shot to death more than a week earlier. Frimpong was being bullied at school, but the reasons for his murder remain unclear. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"As of right now, all indications are that he was trying to live the American dream," the chief said. "He was trying to get ahead by going to school. We have nothing in our investigation to indicate he was involved in any gang activity. Seems like he was just a very good kid."

The tragedy also prompted federal intervention to support the grieving family. President Donald Trump agreed to grant Javits’ mother an emergency visa so she could travel to the United States from Ghana to lay her son to rest.

"The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Nov. 2 post on X.

"Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump, and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately."

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
articles.excerpt:
It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll

Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’

A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for...
articles.body_text:
It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll

Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’

A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.

If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”.

The complaint, which has been seen by the Guardian and is supported by a number of documents, claims an individual “performed domestic work exclusively for Fifa president Gianni Infantino and his wife, Leena Infantino, at their Miami residence, while receiving compensation or benefits through a Fifa-affiliated entity”, and argues that “senior leadership, acting in their official capacity and on behalf of Fifa, have abused the entity’s tax-exemption status”.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

The complaint goes on to argue: “If organisational funds or resources were used to pay for services benefiting a leader’s household, the arrangement raises serious questions about private benefit, financial reporting, compensation, and governance. The materials also raise questions about the accuracy of representations in employment, payroll, tax, and immigration records. We ask the agencies to investigate the underlying records and determine what occurred.” The IRS has been approached for comment.

The news comes as Fifa’s activities, and specifically Infantino’s involvement in the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and his relationship with the Trump White House, are to come under intensified scrutiny from Democratic politicians in the US after the “blue wave” at the midterm elections. A spokesperson for the ranking member of the House judiciary committee, representative Jamie Raskin, said the committee had not requested documents related to the housekeeper but was “looking closely at those developments”.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “Matters related to the Fifa president’s personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the Fifa president personally.”

The complaint, if taken up, would probably take months to complete and commonly the results of IRS investigations are not published. Any action taken as a result, however, would be in the public domain. The complaint was submitted by the Washington DC lawyer Abed Ayoub, who works in immigration law and has served as the national executive director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC). Last year the ADC was part of the campaign Game Over Israel, which called for Israeli football teams to be banned from international competition.

Fifa said: “We urge the media to act responsibly. As Fifa stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president. Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading Fifa will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.”

Infantino has been described by his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, as a “dictator” who “no longer knows any borders”. Blatter, Fifa’s president for 17 years before resigning amid a corruption scandal at the organisation, made the remarks in an interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel. He criticised the FFE scheme, the Fifa peace prize and, most significantly in his opinion, the overturning of Folarin Balogun’s suspension for a red card during the World Cup.

“Fifa is suffering,” Blatter said. “It is currently led by a person who has allowed himself to be blinded.” He described the peace prize as “embarrassing”, saying: “Why would he do something like that? Infantino awards a peace prize to someone who wages war against Iran shortly afterwards?”

In assessing the FFE scheme, which was abandoned after an international outcry, Blatter said: “Infantino no longer knows any borders. He doesn’t understand any of this.” He described the Balogun controversy as “the worst”, saying: “Statutes can be interpreted. But rules of the game must apply to everyone, you can’t interpret them.”

articles.title: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.excerpt:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we kn...
articles.body_text:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.

“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.

“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.

“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.

“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”

Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.

Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

articles.title: Trump planning new military assault or tighter sanctions, say Iranian officials
articles.excerpt:
Regime adviser says Tehran could be forced into pre-emptive strikes if stalemate continues

Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening ec...
articles.body_text:
Regime adviser says Tehran could be forced into pre-emptive strikes if stalemate continues

Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening economic stranglehold that will push Tehran into retaliatory action.

The assessment comes from Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. Mohammadi, who is regarded as a reliable indicator of Ghalibaf’s thinking, cast doubt on the US president’s claim that the military option was off the table. He claimed Washington was preparing for a limited strike and Iran was already preparing a response.

If the US sanctions continued, he said, a comprehensive pre-emptive war would be needed “to increase the cost of sanctions for the enemy”.

Mohammadi described the US response to Iran’s latest proposals on reopening the strait of Hormuz as “not only unsatisfactory but completely deceptive”. “They do not want to release the frozen funds,” he said. “They do not want to lift the sanctions and they do not want to stop the war in Lebanon.”

He also disclosed that Iran had rejected a request from the US vice-president, JD Vance, for a direct meeting with its negotiators before giving a response to Tehran’s conditions for lifting the siege on the strait.

For now, Trump has settled on a strategy of suffocating Iran through economic pressure and tightening the blockade on its oil exports while facilitating those of other Gulf states through Hormuz.

Mohammadi’s assessments suggest some senior Iranians fear Washington’s strategy might work by destabilising the country. The thinking goes that economic turmoil might spark street protests, potentially around the anniversary of nationwide demonstrations that began in late December last year.

On this basis, the Iranian leadership might conclude that the status quo – a “no peace, no war” impasse – was not sustainable and pre-emptive action was required.

Despite Iranian claims that their blockade of the strait is working, there is concern that Brent crude is at a relatively low $93 a barrel, while Saudi oil production is near prewar levels of 9.3m barrels a day. In an attempt to close any loopholes, Iran said it bombed a US radar post on the Omani island of Didamar three days ago.

In another development, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s national security council, said he had told Russia that Iran was not prepared for even a particle of its highly enriched stockpile of uranium to leave the country, saying it might be needed for planned nuclear-powered submarines.

A third senior official, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, warned Europe that any complicity in the US blockade would be “an act of war that will be etched in the nation’s historical memory”.

Tehran has been increasingly clear that US bases in Europe will be targeted if fighting resumes. Rezaei said: “If American planes take off from a distant military base and come to this country to bomb Iran, we will also target that base. We are announcing this now so they have no excuse tomorrow.”

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, gave the impression this week that the policy of economic strangulation was sufficient and described Iran’s demands as unrealistic. However, Trump is under pressure to resolve the crisis before the Democrats take charge of Congress on 3 January.

A Reuters Ipsos poll in the US shows 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation to end the war in Iran. The overwhelming message from the midterm elections was that the conflict was highly unpopular but the Democrats do not have a strategy to end it and open up the strait of Hormuz. This risks leaving the political initiative with the White House, and an increasingly hardline Iranian leadership.

articles.title: Biden ripped for ‘totally delusional’ claim about debate that preceded his 2024 exit
articles.excerpt:
Former President Joe Biden told People Magazine in an interview released Wednesday that his June 2024 presidential debate against then-candidate Donald Trump was not "consequential."

Former President...
articles.body_text:
Former President Joe Biden told People Magazine in an interview released Wednesday that his June 2024 presidential debate against then-candidate Donald Trump was not "consequential."

Former President Joe Biden is facing sharp backlash after dismissing his disastrous 2024 debate performance against President Donald Trump as "not very consequential" — despite dropping out of the presidential race just 24 days later.

When asked about what his "perspective" on the June 27, 2024 debate is now in an interview with People Magazine released Wednesday, Biden suggested he felt his debate performance was inconsequential.

"Look, I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate," Biden told People Magazine. "To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t."

JILL BIDEN SAYS SHE THOUGHT JOE WAS HAVING A STROKE DURING HIS DISASTROUS 2024 DEBATE PERFORMANCE

Former President Joe Biden speaks with moderator Jake Tapper as former first lady Dr. Jill Biden looks on after a presidential debate with Donald Trump in Atlanta, Ga., on June 27, 2024. (Brian Snyder/Reuters)

"But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential," he added.

Biden's comments drew swift criticism on social media on Wednesday.

SOCIAL MEDIA ERUPTS AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALS SHE WAS 'FRIGHTENED' WATCHING JOE'S DISASTROUS DEBATE

"Joe Biden now claims his 2024 presidential debate against President Trump, which forced him to drop out of the race, was not very consequential," former Trump campaign operative Steve Cortes wrote Wednesday in an X post.

"Just 24 days after the 'not very consequential' presidential debate, Joe Biden ended his campaign for President," Cortes added.

Conservative commentator Steve Guest wrote on X that Biden "is TOTALLY delusional."

Meanwhile, former National Republican Senatorial Committee senior adviser Matt Whitlock asserted in a Wednesday post on X that it was actually "the most consequential" presidential debate of all time.

"It was without question the most consequential Presidential debate in history - he [Biden] likely would have stayed the nominee without it," Whitlock said. "But I’m definitely excited for the other hot takes in the book now."

"It was the most lopsided debate in history. C’mon, man!" Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis quipped.

Former U.S. First Lady Dr. Jill Biden revealed that she thought then-President Joe Biden had had a stroke during his 2024 debate with then-candidate Donald Trump. (Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images)

During the presidential debate, Biden stumbled over his words, paused for long periods of time and displayed confused facial expressions.

The Office of Joe and Jill Biden did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

"Biden subsequently dropped out of the presidential race on July 21, 2024, just a few weeks after the debate, amid mounting pressure from Democratic allies to end his re-election bid.

Former first lady Jill Biden notably claimed in a CBS News Sunday Morning interview clip released in May 2026 that she thought her husband was having a stroke on stage during the debate.

Trump's White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Former President Joe Biden and former first lady Jill Biden speak with CNN anchors Jake Tapper and Dana Bash after the CNN presidential debate in Atlanta, Ga., on June 27, 2024. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Additionally, Biden said Sunday that he plans to scale back public appearances promoting his new presidential memoir, "Promise Me, America," due to his cancer battle.

"My presidential memoir, PROMISE ME, AMERICA, is coming out on November 17th. I hope you'll read it. It covers my years as President. The challenges we faced, the decisions I made, and why I made them. It's about who we are as a nation," Biden said in an X post. "What we stand for. And America's role in the world."

"While writing the book, I was diagnosed with cancer, a disease known all too well to millions of Americans and their families," the former president added. "My doctors continue to be encouraged by how I've responded to treatment. And the prayers and kind words and well wishes from so many of you have meant more to me and Jill and our family than you can ever know. Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down."
