articles.title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
articles.excerpt:
An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery

The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump ...
articles.body_text:
An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery

The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.

The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".

"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.

"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.

Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed arch

Last week the project won approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

But US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ruled there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch as litigation plays out.

The Kennedy family filed its complaint under a joint lawsuit brought by the state of Virginia and Washington DC seeking to block construction, arguing that the arch will damage "historically significant sightlines" if erected at the gateway of the cemetery.

The plaintiffs include seven children of Robert and Ethel Kennedy, as well as their grandson - former Democrat congressman Joe Kennedy - and Ted Kennedy's son Edward Kennedy Jr.

It does not include Trump cabinet official Robert F Kennedy Jr, who leads the Department of Health and Human Services.

Their motion moves to intervene in two other lawsuits filed by conservationists and veterans seeking to halt the construction.

They say the arch would be a "permanent denigration" of the gravesites and that the Kennedy offspring "would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended".

The Kennedy family argues the structure "will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family's honor" at the cemetery.

The structure would also "fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites", including the memorials of hundreds of thousands of US veterans, the Kennedys said.

The complaint said that the National Park Service and Interior Department authorised construction on 5 November 2026 without the necessary congressional approval.

The so-called Arc de Trump is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.

Last year, he also added his name to the Kennedy Center, a major Washington DC cultural institution named in honour of JFK.

Trump's name remained on the facade for six months until the addition was ruled illegal and removed.

articles.title: Former West Point cadet sued over alleged drugging, forced abortion of ex-girlfriend: 'Horrifying'
articles.excerpt: Alliance Defending Freedom attorney Erin Hawley says the alleged assault by former West Point cadet Caleb Suh, who pleaded guilty after drugging his pregnant ex-girlfriend and administering abortion p...
articles.body_text:
Alliance Defending Freedom attorney Erin Hawley says the alleged assault by former West Point cadet Caleb Suh, who pleaded guilty after drugging his pregnant ex-girlfriend and administering abortion pills without her consent, was "horrifying."

A former West Point cadet who pleaded guilty to drugging his then-girlfriend and administering abortion pills without her consent, causing a miscarriage, is facing a civil lawsuit that seeks unspecified damages.

Caleb Suh pleaded guilty in June to assault resulting in substantial bodily injury to a dating partner in connection with the March 2022 incident involving the woman, who was also a cadet at the U.S. Military Academy at the time.

Suh studied at two Ivy League universities since the incident, including one where he began attending classes after his guilty plea. He graduated from Cornell University this year and was enrolled as a graduate student at Columbia University when the woman filed a lawsuit Oct. 28.

The woman wanted to have the baby, but Suh did not want her to keep the child. Suh told the judge that he used the woman's identity to set up an online pharmacy account, ordered abortion drugs through the mail, obtained Xanax from a friend to use as a sedative and tricked his girlfriend into drinking what he claimed was a prenatal protein shake. When she fell asleep, Suh inserted the abortion pills into her mouth and vagina.

PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND

Caleb Suh pleaded guilty this summer to the March 2022 assault on the woman, who was also a cadet. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Erin Hawley, a lawyer with the pro-life legal group Alliance Defending Freedom who played a key role in helping overturn Roe v. Wade, said the woman was put in an "absolutely horrific situation."

"She was expecting a child she very much wanted, was drugged and assaulted," Hawley, who is not representing the woman, told Fox News Digital. "The horrifying assault ended up causing the death of her very much wanted child — something no woman should ever have to endure. It has obviously caused a lot of harm and trauma, in addition to the loss of the baby she very much wanted."

"She was drugged and assaulted with abortion pills, even though Mr. Suh knew she very much wanted that child. I expect that he will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law," she added.

Suh left the woman alone and incapacitated and ignored her attempts to reach him once she woke up and noticed that she was bleeding, according to the lawsuit. She was then hospitalized.

As the woman was receiving medical attention, Suh returned to the online pharmacy's website and posted questions about whether doctors could detect the medication he administered, according to the lawsuit.

"She’s suffered a life-changing event that she is still dealing with and will be dealing with for the rest of her life," her lawyer, Russell Kornblith, told The Associated Press last week.

"We hope that by our client coming forward with this lawsuit, it will, at least, ensure that this never happens to anyone else," Kornblith said.

INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Caleb Suh graduated from Cornell University this year and was a graduate student at Columbia University when the woman filed a lawsuit late last month. (TW Farlow/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to Suh's attorney for comment.

During a court hearing in June, Suh said that he was "deeply and immeasurably sorry for my actions and the pain that I have caused."

Suh's sentencing has been postponed until Jan. 21, 2027, at his attorney's request, allowing him to finish the semester at Columbia. Prosecutors did not oppose the delay for Suh's sentencing.

He has also been taking a three-month life skills course for people facing federal charges, his attorney said in a letter to the court.

Suh transferred to Cornell during the 2023-2024 school year. The university said in a statement last week that he answered "no" on an application when asked if he had been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at any previous institution.

The university said West Point noted that he was in good academic standing and was eligible to return. He had been involved in health and medicine at Cornell and wanted to become a physician, according to the university's website.

In September, Suh started a master's program at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health, his lawyer wrote to the judge in his federal case. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that Mailman applicants are not asked about their criminal records but are questioned about whether they have ever been disciplined for student conduct violations or poor academic performance.

Suh’s application never made any mention of past disciplinary proceedings, the person told the outlet.

As the woman was receiving medical attention, Caleb Suh returned to the online pharmacy's website and posted questions about whether doctors could detect the medication he administered (Soumyabrata Roy/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"Regardless of one’s position on abortion, it is not good medicine to allow an abortion drug to be shipped across the country to a dorm room or a home without a woman ever having talked to a doctor," Hawley said.

"The defendant in this case impersonated his girlfriend, had those drugs shipped and then assaulted her with them. That would never have happened if the FDA had done its job in 2023. Hopefully, when the courts do their job and reinstate that safeguard, it won’t continue to happen," she continued, referring to Alliance Defending Freedom's lawsuit challenging the Food and Drug Administration's 2023 decision to remove the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, after the agency had already stopped enforcing the requirement in 2021.

However, the assault occurred in March 2022, before the FDA's 2023 decision. The agency had already announced in April 2021 that it would temporarily stop enforcing the in-person dispensing requirement during the COVID-19 public health emergency. In December 2021, the FDA announced plans to permanently remove the requirement, a change formally implemented in January 2023.

The FDA has said its decision to remove the requirement followed a review of available evidence. Other restrictions, including prescriber certification requirements, remained in place.

Hawley added that the case at West Point would never have happened if that requirement had been in place.

"Horrific incidents like that throughout the country would never have happened if that basic safeguard had been in place," she said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
articles.excerpt:
Watch: Republicans vote to block Hegseth impeachment from reaching full vote

An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisa...
articles.body_text:
Watch: Republicans vote to block Hegseth impeachment from reaching full vote

An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky - for now.

In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".

The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.

His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote.

The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January.

President Trump celebrated the vote in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED".

"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.

After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS.

"My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."

Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

Hegseth: Impeachment effort is "farce" and "stunt"

The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.

Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year.

The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail.

In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval.

The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific  Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated".

Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations".

"This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said.

He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.

But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February.

He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.

articles.title: Kennedy family joins US lawsuits to block Trump’s ‘unlawful’ arch plan
articles.excerpt: Members of the prominent Kennedy family have filed a legal motion to halt the construction of US President Donald Trump’s 76-metre (250ft) “triumphal arch” in Washington, DC, arguing it mars the area ...
articles.body_text:
Members of the prominent Kennedy family have filed a legal motion to halt the construction of US President Donald Trump’s 76-metre (250ft) “triumphal arch” in Washington, DC, arguing it mars the area near the graves of the family’s famous forebears.

On Tuesday, the nine plaintiffs, children and grandchildren of former Senators Robert F Kennedy and Edward M Kennedy, filed a motion to intervene and an accompanying complaint in two existing federal lawsuits to block the arch’s construction.

The project would sit near the final resting places of the late senators, buried alongside their brother, former President John F Kennedy, and the Eternal Flame commemorating him at Arlington National Cemetery.

Plaintiffs argued the proposed arch would “fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites”, a site that draws millions of visitors each year.

The intervention motion was filed by veteran Washington lawyer Norm Eisen and Democracy Defenders Fund, a centre-left legal advocacy group.

It contends that the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior authorised the granite, gold-ornamented structure, dubbed the “Arc de Trump” by critics, without required congressional approval.

The plaintiffs also argue the megastructure would destroy the intentionally designed, century-old line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and the cemetery’s Arlington House across the Memorial Bridge.

The high-profile intervention adds to an already sprawling roster of plaintiffs who have launched legal challenges against the polarising monument, including Vietnam War veterans, a historian, and the governments of the District of Columbia, Virginia and Arlington County.

Last week, District Judge Tanya Chutkan prohibited the Trump administration from breaking ground on the structure for another 14 days following the string of lawsuits.

Building the arch would be a “permanent denigration” of the gravesites, and the Kennedy offspring “would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended”, lawyers for the relatives wrote on Tuesday.

The project is just one component of the president’s effort to remodel much of Washington, DC, alongside a historic golf course renovation and threats to demolish the Kennedy Center.

But with Democrats seizing control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections, the overhauls may be set for heightened scrutiny.

Speaking on behalf of the Kennedy family, Rory and Maxwell Kennedy, children of the late senator Robert F Kennedy, said the action is about “protecting sacred spaces that belong to the American people”. They said several members of their slain family are “among the more than 400,000 veterans and family members buried or honored on this hallowed ground”.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, a Trump appointee who is estranged from much of his family,  did not join the litigation.

articles.title: Labor won’t scrap ABC and SBS ombudsmen in favour of external body as suggested by antisemitism envoy
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Jillian Segal suggested ‘transferring’ powers in updated report released a fortnight ago but government sources note media regulator already exists

Get our breaking news email, free app or...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Jillian Segal suggested ‘transferring’ powers in updated report released a fortnight ago but government sources note media regulator already exists

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Albanese government won’t follow a suggestion by the antisemitism envoy to scrap the ABC and SBS ombudsmen and replace them with an external oversight body.

In a list of updated priorities released last month, Segal proposed an “external independent ombudsman” to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of the war in Gaza and to ensure publicly funded broadcasters were “held accountable to their own stated standards of accuracy and impartiality”.

“Many in the Jewish community remain concerned that coverage they perceive as one-directional may contribute to a negative – and even hostile – view by audiences of those who support Israel, or have sympathy for it,” Segal said in her updated plan to combat antisemitism.

Segal said the government should consider “transferring” responsibilities from the ABC and SBS ombudsmen to an “external independent ombudsman consistent with other sectors such as telecommunications and banking”.

The ABC said at the time its complaints process was “the most robust and transparent in the Australian media” and both broadcasters stated they were subject to external review by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (Acma).

This week, government sources noted that Acma already acted as an external independent regulator that could investigate complaints if they needed to be escalated beyond the ABC and SBS ombudsmen.

A spokesperson for the federal communications minister, Anika Wells, on Wednesday thanked Segal for her work and said there was no place for antisemitism in Australia.

It was an evil “that tears at the fabric of our country … [and] puts the peaceful, free and equal society we cherish at risk”, they said.

It is understood Labor could consider changes in response to recommendations from the royal commission into antisemitism that is scheduled to report in mid-December. The commission, headed by former high court judge Virginia Bell, was established after the antisemitic Bondi beach massacre in December 2025.

“The government will soon receive the final report from the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion,” Wells’ spokesperson said on Wednesday.

“[It] will continue to work with the special envoy, the Jewish community and all Australians to combat antisemitism and strengthen our social cohesion.”

Segal’s latest suggestion regarding the ABC and SBS received a mixed response a fortnight ago.

Alex Ryvchin, the co-chief executive of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, welcomed Segal’s suggestions, warning meaningful oversight of coverage by public broadcasters could only be achieved “through external accountability”.

But the progressive Jewish Council of Australia criticised the envoy’s new plan as “Trumpian”, arguing it threatened freedom of speech and democratic rights.

The Australian Palestine Advocacy Network criticised attempts to conflate legitimate criticism of Israel with antisemitism and stated: “Speaking out against Israel’s ongoing atrocities is the prerogative of anyone who believes in human dignity and human rights.”

Segal in October wrote that the “independence of public broadcasters must, of course, be protected”.

“That independence, however, does not – and should not – amount to a right to be free from external scrutiny and empirical review. Indeed, ensuring that the processes withstand fair scrutiny can only increase confidence.”

The ABC ombudsman has previously investigated public complaints related to coverage of the Middle East and the war in Gaza, including the Israeli president’s visit to Australia and a press club address by the Israeli ambassador.

ABC Alumni, which represents hundreds of former staff, has said that since October 2023 the ABC ombudsman has upheld four out of thousands of complaints of bias or inaccuracy relating to Middle East coverage.

Acma, “to which dissatisfied complainants can appeal, has upheld none”, the group said in a statement, adding it was “outraged at the continued insistence by Jillian Segal … that the ABC and SBS, Australia’s most trusted news outlets, are contributing to antisemitism”.

In her first report in mid-2025, Segal initially proposed the special envoy be given powers to monitor media organisations to encourage “accurate, fair and responsible reporting” to ensure impartiality and balance and to avoid “accepting false or distorted narratives”.

She then told the royal commission into antisemitism in mid-2026 she wanted a new “oversight” committee that could give ABC and SBS coverage a “tick” or “guidance”.

Segal told Senate estimates this week she was concerned about “the tone [and] the frequency of reporting about Gaza from the ABC”.

articles.title: Underworld figure Mick Gatto gave CFMEU official gold bracelet after construction site assault, Big Build royal commission told
articles.excerpt:
Former CFMEU official Paul Tzimas tells inquiry he suffered fractured ankle and a colleague was left with major injuries and severe PTSD

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A...
articles.body_text:
Former CFMEU official Paul Tzimas tells inquiry he suffered fractured ankle and a colleague was left with major injuries and severe PTSD

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A former CFMEU official has told a royal commission that underworld figure Mick Gatto attended a meeting that was called after the union official and a colleague were seriously assaulted at a construction site, claiming the underworld figure later offered him a gold bracelet.

Paul Tzimas is the first witness associated with the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union to appear before the royal commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria.

Tzimas told the commission on Wednesday that he received a fractured ankle and a colleague was left with a broken eye socket, damage to his teeth, severe PTSD and the partial loss of his vision after they were assaulted by people linked to the builders and developers at a construction site.

No other details were given about where and when the assault occurred, but Tzimas agreed that he believed the people who assaulted him may have been linked to an outlaw bikie gang.

Tzimas, a former CFMEU official who left the union in January and is now unemployed, told the commission that about a week after the assault a meeting was called between union officials and the builders, who also arranged for Gatto to attend.

He said Gatto was known to work for developers and builders in order to resolve issues with their projects.

Tzimas said that Gatto later gifted him a gold bracelet, which he initially refused.

He agreed with counsel assisting Chris Carr that he first knocked back the gift as he knew it could be “perceived as inappropriate for someone in your position to receive a gift from someone on the other side of the fence”.

Tzimas also agreed with Carr that he knew the bracelet was not a “worthless trinket” but that, after discussing with Gatto why he was being gifted it, he decided to take it.

“Mick had expressed that – especially because I refused it – that it wasn’t his way of … trying to earn any favour.

“He said he had had a poor opinion of me as an official, he believed he probably judged me a bit harshly, and this was an olive branch so to speak, for people he considered a friend.

Tzimas said he was aware other union officials also received gold bracelets from Gatto.

Tzimas was also asked about a letter the CFMEU wrote on behalf of a man convicted of manslaughter who was seeking parole that confirmed he would be offered employment.

He told the commission that he was unclear why the union assisted the man but said “his dad at the time was a union delegate … so that probably holds some sway as well”.

Carr also read the names of 15 men to Tzimas and asked whether all of them were union members and affiliated with bikie gangs. Tzimas agreed that 11 of them were.

A level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury, north of Melbourne, is the focus of the commission’s November hearings.

Tzimas attended the work site as part of union action that eventually halted construction.

He also attended a meeting between project managers and the union officials at CFMEU headquarters on 7 June 2022 that eventually resulted in work recommencing on the site.

The commission has previously heard that in that meeting the union demanded that its own health and safety representative, and union affiliated traffic management and labour hire companies, had to be installed on the Gap Road project in order for work to resume.

The hearing before commissioner Christopher Kourakis continues.

articles.title: Stacy Keach dead at 85 as ‘Mike Hammer’ star’s wife shares emotional tribute
articles.excerpt:
Hollywood mourns the loss of legendary actor Stacy Keach, best known for his iconic role as detective Mike Hammer.

Stacy Keach, the legendary actor whose unmistakable voice and powerful performances ...
articles.body_text:
Hollywood mourns the loss of legendary actor Stacy Keach, best known for his iconic role as detective Mike Hammer.

Stacy Keach, the legendary actor whose unmistakable voice and powerful performances captivated generations of Americans, is being remembered by his beloved wife as a devoted husband, loving father and courageous fighter after his death at 85.

Keach, best known for portraying the hard-boiled private detective Mike Hammer and for his celebrated work on stage and screen, died Tuesday, Nov. 10, at his family home in Magdalenka, Poland.

His wife, Małgosia Tomassi Keach, shared an emotional statement announcing his passing following a lengthy battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure.

PATRICK STEWART, LEGENDARY 'STAR TREK' AND 'X-MEN' ACTOR, DIES AT 86

Stacy Keach attends the Los Angeles premiere of "Taking Care," hosted by Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen, at Harmony Gold Preview House on April 16, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images)

"It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach," she said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

"After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength."

She remembered her husband as a man whose remarkable resilience extended far beyond the characters he brought to life on-screen.

"He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life," she continued.

Rana Ghadban, Matt LeBlanc, Stacy Keach and Malgosia Tomassi Keach attend a Hollywood event. (Penske Media via Getty Images)

"Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family."

For millions of television viewers, Keach will forever be remembered as Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer, the tough-talking private investigator he portrayed with grit, charisma and an unmistakable screen presence.

EVA MARIE SAINT, OSCAR-WINNING ‘ON THE WATERFRONT’ AND ‘NORTH BY NORTHWEST’ STAR, DEAD AT 102

James Spader as Raymond "Red" Reddington and Stacy Keach as Robert Vesco are pictured in "The Hyena," episode 1004 of The Blacklist. (Scott Gries/NBC via Getty Images)

But his extraordinary career stretched far beyond the detective series. A gifted Shakespearean actor, Keach tackled some of theater's most demanding roles, including Hamlet, Richard III and King Lear. He also earned a Golden Globe for his portrayal of Ernest Hemingway.

His television appearances included "Blue Bloods," "Titus" and "Prison Break," while his film credits ranged from "The Long Riders" to "Nebraska" and "The Bourne Legacy."

Keach also appeared in the Biblical miniseries "Jesus of Nazareth," portraying the criminal Barabbas.

In 2017, Keach suffered a heart attack while performing in a one-man production about Ernest Hemingway at Chicago's Goodman Theatre, an ordeal that forced the cancellation of the show's run.

Throughout a career spanning more than six decades, Keach earned admiration not only for his versatility but also for the unmistakable voice and commanding presence that made him one of Hollywood's most recognizable performers.

Yet for those closest to him, his greatest legacy was the love he shared with his family.

"His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives," his wife said. "But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever."

Keach is survived by his wife, their children, Karolina and Shannon, and their extended family. His family's farewell was signed with profound love and sorrow by Małgosia, Karolina, Shannon, their grandchildren and spouses.The Associated Press contributed to this reporting.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

articles.title: Foo Fighters interrupt Sydney concert to pay tribute to Beaconsfield miner Todd Russell

Dave Grohl tells Sydney crowd Russell, whose death was announced this week, was a ‘big’ hero of his

Todd Russell, Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor, dies aged 54 due to illness

Get our breaking ne...
articles.body_text:
Dave Grohl tells Sydney crowd Russell, whose death was announced this week, was a ‘big’ hero of his

Todd Russell, Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor, dies aged 54 due to illness

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A solemn moment has broken up an otherwise raucous Foo Fighters Australian concert as the band’s frontman made a lengthy on-stage tribute to Beaconsfield survivor Todd Russell.

The US band are touring Australia for the 16th time in their 32-year history and Tuesday night’s Sydney show coincided with the news of Russell’s death at the age of 54.

The Tasmanian mine collapsed on Anzac Day 20 years ago and trapped Russell a kilometre below ground with co-worker Brant Webb.

The pair were presumed dead in the disaster, which killed a third miner, Larry Knight.

The two survivors were trapped in a vehicle underground and their 14-day rescue effort became global news.

When the duo were asked what supplies they needed, Russell asked for an iPod with Foo Fighters music to keep his spirits alive as loud drilling took place for the rescue effort.

The Foo Fighters frontman, Dave Grohl, told the Accor Stadium crowd his band had a funny relationship with the Beaconsfield miners.

While the duo were trapped, Grohl sent a message to say he had two tickets and two beers waiting for them for any Foo Fighters show when they got out of the mine.

He kept his promise and met the pair backstage at the Sydney Opera House show later in 2006.

Grohl wrote the duo a song the night before, called Ballad of the Beaconsfield Miners.

At Tuesday’s show, band members left Grohl standing on stage as a picture of Russell appeared on screen and the singer recalled their get-together 20 years earlier.

“Afterwards we all went to the bar and we had the beers I promised, and I got so drunk I promised I’d put [Ballad of the Beaconsfield Miners] on our next record,” he said.

“And I did. I’m glad I did because I’ve met a few heroes in my life but that was a big one, so I’m doing this one tonight for Todd Russell.”

Russell’s death came one week after he announced a move home to “see out his days” following an illness.

articles.title: GOP-led House report slams systemic failures in handling of Epstein case
articles.excerpt: Congressional Republicans are pressing for renewed investigations into sex crimes cases involving disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein and accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, accusing authorities of mishandl...
articles.body_text:
Congressional Republicans are pressing for renewed investigations into sex crimes cases involving disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein and accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, accusing authorities of mishandling the case for decades.

The US House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform on Tuesday released a new 137-page report marking the most comprehensive investigation yet by lawmakers into the federal government’s handling of the Epstein saga.

The findings condemned federal investigators and prosecutors in South Florida and Washington for alleged negligence, which the committee said allowed the late sex offender’s abuse to go unchecked as far back as 2005, when Epstein’s crimes first came to light in Palm Beach, Florida.

“What we found was both heartbreaking and infuriating,” Republican Representative James Comer of Kentucky, who chairs the committee, said in a video address.

“These women endured unimaginable abuse, and the federal government failed them at nearly every turn,” he added. “Had the government done its job, much of this abuse could have been prevented.”

The committee, which currently holds a Republican majority, is the House’s main investigative panel and has the power to subpoena witnesses and documents.

Democrats will take control of the chamber in January after a historic victory in the November 3 midterm elections, and California Representative Robert Garcia, the committee’s top Democrat, formally announced his bid to chair it in a letter to colleagues on Thursday.

The latest findings cap a 15-month Republican-led congressional inquiry that involved 19 transcribed interviews and depositions, subpoenas to federal agencies, financial institutions and Epstein’s estate, and an extensive review of financial records.

Its conclusions asserted that a combination of bureaucratic indifference, missed warnings and compromised plea deals consistently shielded Epstein and his associates while denying justice to their victims.

In one such instance, GOP lawmakers sharply rebuked a controversial 2007 non-prosecution agreement in South Florida that effectively shelved Epstein’s federal case after he pleaded guilty to lesser state offences.

Florida prosecutors, working alongside the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), at the time granted him a lenient 18-month sentence alongside extensive work-release privileges, a period during which he continued to abuse women, according to the report.

The panel ascribed the outcomes to “poor judgment” and Epstein’s influence, while flagging potential conflicts of interest involving two former prosecutors, Matthew Menchel and Bruce Reinhart, then employed in the US Attorney’s Office (USAO) for the Southern District of Florida.

“Former US Attorney Alexander Acosta’s hands-off approach to the investigation and his failures to oversee the daily involvement of those at the USAO left the investigation in the hands of potential Epstein loyalists,” the report read.

Separately, the report blamed understaffing and institutional dysfunction at the New York federal jail where Epstein died by alleged suicide in August 2019, revealing that guards skipped 12 patrols and three inmate counts, failing to perform the required 30-minute safety checks.

Epstein was being housed in the Metropolitan Correctional Center’s (MCC) Special Housing Unit when his cell was left unmonitored for nearly eight hours the night he died.

According to testimony provided to the committee by Tova Noel, a former MCC correctional officer who performed Epstein’s final cell check, the critical lapse was simply “the MCC way”.

The committee’s report defined the jail’s institutional culture as one in which “departures from established policies and procedures had become routine”.

To deliver long-awaited accountability, the Republican-led committee urged the Department of Justice (DOJ) to interview or re-interview key witnesses and to investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity. The report includes testimony from a witness who accused two high-profile figures of abuse: former Miami Beach Mayor Philip Levine and French celebrity hairstylist Frederic Fekkai.

“The evidence we uncovered makes clear that the Department of Justice must interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records,” Comer said in a statement, adding that “Congress must also pass legislation protecting the ability of individuals with knowledge of sexual abuse and survivors to speak freely about these crimes, regardless of nondisclosure agreements”.

The report also dismissed the committee Democrats’ probe into Trump as an “unfounded witch hunt”, saying they were “obsessed with trying to implicate President Trump and insinuate that he was involved in the crimes of Epstein and Maxwell”.

Questions remain about whether the DOJ provided all required records under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, a measure passed by a near-unanimous Congress and signed into law by US President Donald Trump in November 2025.

The rushed nature of the disclosure led to “deficient redaction” that “exposed sensitive information” belonging to victims, the GOP-led report added.

The panel further recommended measures granting survivors access to unredacted personal files and urged passing the Survivor’s Voice Protection Act to prohibit using non-disclosure agreements to conceal sexual abuse.

articles.title: Rising Tide banned from using council land for protests at world’s largest coal port in Newcastle
articles.excerpt:
NSW premier Chris Minns warned council would be complicit in any ‘illegal activities that occur at these protests’

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Newcastle council – h...
articles.body_text:
NSW premier Chris Minns warned council would be complicit in any ‘illegal activities that occur at these protests’

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Newcastle council – home to the world’s largest coal port – has banned a climate group from holding any events on its land after consulting the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, who warned the council would be complicit in any “illegal activities that occur at these protests”.

On Tuesday night the council’s independent lord mayor, Gavin Morris, used his casting vote to ban any licensing of Rising Tide’s events, claiming in a mayoral minute that the group had “broken the trust and faith of the Newcastle community” by defying police directions during past protests.

Rising Tide holds an annual event where thousands of protesters wade into the port with kayaks and rafts over the course of the six-day protest to blockade coal ships. The protest includes camping on council land and a music festival where major Australian bands have played, including Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett.

The protest is run to draw attention to the group’s demands for the immediate cancellation of all new fossil fuel projects, the end of coal exports from Newcastle by 2030, and taxing fossil fuel profits at 78% to fund community and industrial transitions.

During the 2024 protest, the Minns government attempted to stop the event from going ahead after it put in place around the port a four-day maritime exclusion zone, which criminalised entering the water. But just as the protest was kicking off, the supreme court found the government had acted improperly and ruled the exclusion zone invalid after Rising Tide challenged it.

During the event 173 protesters were charged, but in August police withdrew charges against 125 of those people.

For the 2025 blockade, the government and the police did not make an attempt to stop the protest from going ahead. Police arrested and charged 129 protesters who entered the water at the 2025 event, which stopped three coal ships from entering the port. They remain before the courts.

The group has a smaller paddle-out event planned for this Saturday ahead of their annual protest, which will next be held in February.

The group were before the NSW supreme court on Wednesday for the Saturday event after the police knocked back their application for a form 1 permit. The court is expected to decide later on Wednesday if it will support the police’s decision to not provide the protesters protection from being charged under the Summary Offences Act.

Minns wrote to the council ahead of the motion being passed saying it was “not possible for the council to distance itself from the illegal activities that occur at these protests”.

He wrote that the protest is only possible through the council’s licensing of the events at a local park.

“While I completely understand the right to protest and the need to protect lawful protest, we need to ensure that protests occur in a safe way, and not in a manner which disrupts shipping traffic at the Port of Newcastle,” he wrote.

“Rising Tide has a history that indicates their intent is to disrupt the shipping channel of your harbour without regard for the law.

“I acknowledge the independence of your council to make decisions. However I believe that formally endorsing this protest will put lives at risk and make NSW police’s job impossible.”

The minister for the Hunter and police, Yasmin Catley, who was also consulted on the motion, wrote to the council supporting its decision, labelling Rising Tide “bad faith actors”.

“They flouted the ruling of the supreme court in 2024 prohibiting their assembly and ignored the statutory requirements for holding a protected protest entirely in 2025 resulting in 141 arrests.”

A Rising Tide spokesperson, Zack Schofield, said: “Desperate attempts like this to suppress protest are proof that Rising Tide has been effective in building pressure against the world’s largest coal port.

“We intend to exercise our right to protest because the world is burning, it is flooding, our climate is collapsing and time is running out. Paddle for the Planet will go ahead this Saturday at Horseshoe Beach, as will future protests.”

articles.title: Mullin vows ‘zero change’ on immigration after Republicans suffer crushing midterm losses
articles.excerpt:
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin discusses the future of the Trump administration’s immigration policy and the viability of working with Democrats on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

Department of Homeland Securi...
articles.body_text:
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin discusses the future of the Trump administration’s immigration policy and the viability of working with Democrats on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin delivered a blunt message on immigration policy Tuesday, promising "zero change" following midterm elections that dealt a crushing blow to the Republican Party.

Mullin made the remarks during an appearance on Fox News' "The Ingraham Angle," where host Laura Ingraham brought up President Donald Trump suggesting Republicans work with Democrats.

"Amnesty will never be on the table," Mullin said.

WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS

FILE — DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin ruled out immigration amnesty and pledged continued deportations after Republican losses in the midterm elections. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

He noted that the agency has been deporting roughly 3,600 individuals a day and has no plans to slow down.

"We haven't slowed down at all. We've re-prioritize what we're doing by going after the worst of the worst, by getting the murderers and the rapists and child predators and drug bankers and cartel members," he added.

While Democrats secured majorities in both the House and Senate during the midterm elections, Mullin said Republicans cannot trust the opposing party to work with them.

"You can't trust the Democrat Party we've been working with at all. You can't, because nothing's enough for them," he said.

He also criticized the Democratic Party's leadership, pointing to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and accusing the group of wanting to "defund the country."

"You got DSA that's running the Democrat Party right now. They want to defund my agency, the Department of Homeland Security," he said.

BORDER DEM POISED TO WIELD ICE PURSE STRINGS REJECTS SOCIALIST ‘DEFUND’ PUSH

FILE — Mullin said strong border security remains critical to national security as he pledged no slowdown in deportations following Republicans’ midterm losses.

"You want to defund the country that is the agency that's tasked with keeping our homeland safe? Doesn’t make any sense," he added.

Mullin also recalled Trump's comments about using his veto power if Democrats pass measures he opposes.

"The president has made it very clear he controls the veto. So if they were to send something over that the president and the Republicans don't agree with, he can veto it, and he will veto it," he said.

"The president will not sign anything that isn't in the right movement for this country and the Republican Party."

Mullin also argued that maintaining a strong immigration policy is imperative to national security.

FILE — DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed to maintain strict border enforcement and ruled out amnesty after Democrats swept the midterm elections. (AP Photo/Eugene Garcia, File)

"You can't have a secured nation and you can't have a secured city if you don't know who's in your country," he said.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Baby No. 4 joins an established crew at home with Sterling Skye, Bronze and Golden Raye.

BRITTANY MAHOMES GOES COWGIRL WHILE DRAGGING PATRICK MAHOMES OUT TO STAGECOACH

Sterling arrived in February 2021, followed by Patrick "Bronze" Lavon III in November 2022, and Golden Raye in January 2025 during the Chiefs' playoff bye week.

Speculation is already mounting over whether the fourth child keeps the precious-metals naming streak alive.

While most comments congratulated the couple, some couldn't help but chime in from a football perspective.

Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes attend the 2024 TIME100 Gala at Jazz at Lincoln Center in New York City on April 25, 2024. (Kristina Bumphrey/Variety)

"Pat trying to break every record a QB has. Going after Phillip Rivers record for kids ... "

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Meanwhile, Chiefs general manager Brett Veach beat the 4 p.m. trade deadline cutoff to hand Patrick a fresh target in slot receiver Josh Downs. The Chiefs enter the second half of the 2026 season firmly in the AFC hunt.

In Patrick's 10th NFL season, Kansas City has had to navigate a tight divisional race alongside a stubborn Denver Broncos squad.

Patrick Mahomes of the Kansas City Chiefs talks with his wife Brittany Mahomes prior to the game against the Washington Commanders at Arrowhead Stadium on Oct. 27, 2025, in Kansas City, Missouri. (Jamie Squire/Getty Images)

articles.title: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
articles.excerpt:
El Salvador's president posted a video on X of the strikes on a complex he said is the headquarters of 400 Mawozo

The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salva...
articles.body_text:
El Salvador's president posted a video on X of the strikes on a complex he said is the headquarters of 400 Mawozo

The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said.

The infamous 400 Mawozo gang, which is known for kidnappings and intimidation tactics, was targeted in a ground and air attack at a complex on the outskirts of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince.

It is El Salvador's first military action on a Haitian target since it deployed more than 2,000 soldiers there last month, as part of a mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran technicians.

Haiti has been plagued by gang violence for years, with heavily armed groups controlling large parts of the capital, and beyond.

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced the news on X, external, boasting that most of the gang members fled without trying to fight.

"We destroyed the house of [gang leader] Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters," he wrote on Tuesday.

The post was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex, reportedly in the suburb of Croix-des-Bouquets, the gang's stronghold.

As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

Several media outlets have reported that as many as 20 people were killed, however that has not been confirmed by authorities. There has also been no official confirmation of the extent of the damage at the property, with Haitians questioning whether it has been destroyed or just damaged.

The Miami Herald reports that the gang's leader, Wilson "Lanmò San Jou" Joseph, was not there at the time.

The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the gang's headquarters.

Salvadoran troops have become a regular sight in Port-au-Prince

Haiti's National Police drone task force was involved in the attack, supported by Salvadoran soldiers, the Miami Herald reports, citing several sources.

Posting on X after the strikes, Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé thanked the Salvadoran military's commitment "in the fight against gangs", and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority".

Some 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were deployed to Haiti last month after four air force technicians were abducted at gunpoint while food shopping in October.

El Salvador's right-wing president has vowed to bring the men home alive and warned the gang to release them immediately or face sustained pressure from his military.

The four abducted men were working as part of the GSF, made up of troops from several nations, initially led by soldiers from Chad.

President Bukele's move to send thousands of Salvadoran troops to Haiti has raised concerns, with critics saying they are not all working within the command structure of the GSF. It has raised questions about the operational legitimacy and legality of their actions in the Caribbean nation.

Amnesty International has urged both countries to "ensure all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law".

Such concerns do not appear to phase Bukele, however, who continues to directly warn and target the gang leaders.

The attack on the supposed gang headquarters seemingly came after a user on X had urged Bukele to attack the complex.

"Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we'll destroy it," he replied to the post, which has now been taken down, apparently for violating X's rules.

The 400 Mawozo gang is the largest criminal organisation in Haiti, and known for kidnappings, extortion, murders and arms trafficking.

Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and remains largely under gang control.

At least 5,700 people have been killed or injured there by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year alone, the United Nations has said.

El Salvador has recorded huge reductions in gang violence under President Bukele as part of a sweeping crackdown, and he has vowed to do the same in Haiti.

However, human rights groups have argued that the way he has done it is unlawful, with the open-ended extension of emergency laws, the treatment of detainees in El Salvador's high-security mega-prison and the mass trials of alleged gang members.

articles.title: Two white students at University of Mississippi make monkey gestures in Ring video
articles.excerpt:
Women are reportedly upstairs neighbors of three Black students, including one who uploaded video to TikTok

Two white students at the University of Mississippi were captured making offensive monkey g...
articles.body_text:
Women are reportedly upstairs neighbors of three Black students, including one who uploaded video to TikTok

Two white students at the University of Mississippi were captured making offensive monkey gestures in a widely panned Ring video that has prompted a school investigation.

On Saturday, freshman Jakiyra Metcalf uploaded the surveillance clip from her apartment door to TikTok, showing one woman thumping her chest and babbling like a monkey. Another woman jumped into the camera’s view and mimicked the primate noises.

The video, which has nearly 13m views, drew outrage over the racist connotation.

“This is absolutely disgusting and unacceptable. College is supposed to be a place where young adults can learn, grow, and feel safe,” Metcalf’s mother, Tasha Bolton, wrote Saturday on Facebook. According to Bolton, her daughter lives with two Black roommates and the women seen in the video are her upstairs neighbors.

The family is not yet speaking publicly about the ordeal, said Bolton’s husband, Brooks Bolton.

Alaina Kunes, 18, who was in the video, issued an apology in a statement released by a Chicago law firm, while insisting her behavior was not related to race.

“I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color,” Kunes said. “I have apologized to the women, and I pray they will forgive me.”

Kunes continued: “Over the past several days, my family and I have received death threats and harassment. I am grateful for the authorities working to ensure our safety. As I intend to cooperate fully with the University’s investigation, I ask for privacy for my family. I understand the seriousness of this situation and remain committed to taking responsibility and learning from this embarrassing ordeal.”

Shawnboda Mead, vice-chancellor for student affairs at the university, condemned the video in a Sunday statement.

“Every student deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued at the University of Mississippi. Racism and actions that disparage people because of an aspect of their identity have no place in our campus community,” she said.

Mead also advised the campus to refrain from sharing unverified information about who was involved in the incident.

The school has reached out to the affected students to offer support and hear their concerns, she said.

A university spokesperson did not reply to a Tuesday inquiry about the women’s enrollment status and whether any disciplinary action had been taken.

The school has seen troubling incidents of racism in the past. In 2014, fraternity members at the University of Mississippi hung a noose around a statue that commemorated the school’s first Black student.

A decade later, at a pro-Palestine demonstration, some white male counter-protesters directed monkey noises at a Black female protester.

articles.title: House Republicans block effort to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth
articles.excerpt:
Trump ally, accused of an array of illegal acts, had earlier condemned impeachment push as ‘a farce and a stunt’

House Republicans on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, rejecting alle...
articles.body_text:
Trump ally, accused of an array of illegal acts, had earlier condemned impeachment push as ‘a farce and a stunt’

House Republicans on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, rejecting allegations that the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of the Iran war and other conflicts globally.

The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.

Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman who lost his primary after breaking with the president, had proposed impeaching Hegseth in September, alleging an array of illegal acts, including killing civilians in Iran, launching unauthorized operations in Venezuela and Yemen, and retaliating against a Democratic senator.

Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Their motion succeeded on Tuesday, by a 211-204 vote, largely along party lines. Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the motion, along with all Democrats.

Trump, who was twice impeached, celebrated what he hailed as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot’ and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote.

“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump said on Truth Social. “They must be stopped!”

The Pentagon, meanwhile, declared “total victory”.

“The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House judiciary committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” Sean Parnell, a department spokesperson, wrote in a social media post.

Tuesday’s vote is unlikely to be the final word on efforts to remove Hegseth from office, after Democrats won decisive majorities in the November midterm elections. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take control of the chamber in January, has backed the push to impeach Hegseth, accusing the embattled secretary of having “undermined America’s national security”.

The resolution’s downfall took place hours after Hegseth held a defiant press conference at the Pentagon, where he dismissed the impeachment effort as a “political spectacle” orchestrated by the ousted Kentucky congressman.

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.

The conflict with Iran has proven divisive with Republicans, and ahead of the midterms, small but growing numbers voted with Democrats on war powers resolutions intended to force Trump to bring the hostilities to a close. Warren Davidson, one of the House Republicans who voted for such resolutions, said he nonetheless rejected the idea of impeaching Hegseth.

“It’s an effort to blame-shift on to Hegseth Congress’s failure and President Trump’s decision,” Davidson said in an interview.

“I think Hegseth has been incredibly effective at restoring morale for the active-duty force, restoring the warrior ethos, the proper focus to the military that they exist to fight and win wars.”

The defense secretary, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer, has been one of the most pugnacious members of Trump’s second term cabinet, and taken an unusually heavy handed approach to managing the US military. Hegseth has orchestrated the departure of top generals, blocked the promotions of scores of officers, many of them women and people of color, and implemented new rules that prompted much of the press corps to leave the Pentagon.

He has also become the public face of some of the administration’s most politically costly policies, particularly the Iran war, which has dragged on for months while putting upward pressure on petroleum prices and played into Democrats’s hands in last week’s midterms.

Massie’s resolution outlined eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, including attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and spurning a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict.

It also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary.

The final two impeachment articles target Hegseth’s involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House.

Had the impeachment resolution passed, it would have had to be approved by the Senate, which Republicans control by a 53-seat margin. It is unclear if it would have had enough votes to pass, or if the Republican leader John Thune would have even put it up for consideration.

articles.title: US House Republicans reject effort to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth
articles.excerpt: Republicans in the United States House of Representatives have nixed an effort to advance the impeachment of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, following a midterm election in which voters vented frustra...
articles.body_text:
Republicans in the United States House of Representatives have nixed an effort to advance the impeachment of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, following a midterm election in which voters vented frustrations over the Iran war Hegseth has helped spearhead.

The lower house of the US Congress voted in favour of a motion to refer the impeachment charges to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee in a procedural vote on Tuesday, effectively killing an effort to remove Hegseth from his position led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie.

That push also won support from Democratic representatives, setting up a test of whether Republican lawmakers would break with the Trump administration and distance themselves from the unpopular war after a rebuke at the polls.

The final vote on Tuesday was 211 in favour and 204 against, with Massie the lone Republican to vote against it. The result means that Republicans will be able to slow-walk the process and can avoid a direct vote on the eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, which cover issues such as the Iran war.

“The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!” Trump said in a social media post following the vote. “Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favour of Pete.”

Regardless of the outcome of Tuesday’s vote, an impeachment conviction in the US Senate, where it would require a two-thirds vote and Republicans have a 53-seat majority, was seen as unlikely.

Massie’s resolution included eight separate articles of impeachment, accusing the combative Pentagon chief of launching an illegal war against Iran without congressional approval and overseeing a campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking vessels that legal scholars say are extrajudicial killings.

Hegseth has denounced the resolution as “sabotage” and a “farce”, while US President Donald Trump and prominent members of his administration expressed their continued support for him.

Speculation about Hegseth’s position within the administration has circulated as polls suggest that voters partly blame the war for surging prices of goods such as gasoline and groceries, and has grown stronger after Republicans faced punishing losses in the midterm elections.

“Is he being truthful in the way the war is going?” outgoing Republican Senator Joni Ernst said of Hegseth on Tuesday.

articles.title: American Airlines plane nearly hit by Air France jet after takeoff at LAX
articles.excerpt: Aviation expert and former airline captain Steven Arroyo breaks down the frighteningly close encounter between an American Airlines aircraft and an Air France plane at Los Angeles International Airpor...
articles.body_text:
Aviation expert and former airline captain Steven Arroyo breaks down the frighteningly close encounter between an American Airlines aircraft and an Air France plane at Los Angeles International Airport recently — and what passengers must know.

Two passenger jets operated by Air France and American Airlines came dangerously close in the air after departing from Los Angeles International Airport recently.

The incident happened at about 12:20 a.m. on Nov. 7 after the Air France aircraft made a turn it had not been cleared to make, according to a statement the Federal Aviation Administration provided to Fox News Digital.

"The crew of Air France Flight 28 made an unauthorized turn after departing Los Angeles International Airport and went into the path of another aircraft that departed from a parallel runway," the FAA said.

JET PLUNGES 27,000 FEET IN 10 MINUTES AS OXYGEN MASKS SUDDENLY DROP ABOARD FLIGHT

Air traffic control audio captured the tense exchange as controllers worked to redirect the flights.

"Air France 028 heavy, fly heading of 270 immediately," a controller can be heard telling the Air France crew.

An Air France plane veered off its expected course recently (not pictured) after taking off from LAX and flew dangerously close to an American Airlines plane that had also just taken off.  (iStock)

Moments later, the controller issued a traffic alert to American Airlines Flight 1660, warning its pilots that another aircraft was directly ahead and less than a mile away.

"Traffic alert, traffic 12 o'clock, less than a mile, maintain 2,000," the controller said.

"OK, we'll go back to 2,000," an American Airlines pilot responded.

Fox News Digital reached out to the two airlines for comment.

"Air France departed from the north side of Los Angeles Airport on a parallel runway from where an American Airlines aircraft took off," Steven Arroyo, an aviation expert and retired airline captain based in Florida, observed to Fox News Digital (he was not connected to the incident).

"All of a sudden, unannounced, the Air France aircraft made … an unauthorized left-hand turn toward the American Airlines aircraft," he said.

An American Airlines plane (not pictured) received an alert from traffic control that another aircraft was directly ahead and less than a mile away. (iStock)

"They came within 400 feet of each other and less than one mile. That is dangerously close," Arroyo noted.

Once the immediate conflict was addressed, the controller questioned the Air France crew about why the aircraft had turned.

"Air France 028 heavy, you were instructed to climb via SID, not turn to a heading," the controller said.

A SID, or Standard Instrument Departure, is a published departure procedure that can be assigned to an aircraft as part of its flight clearance, according to the FAA's air traffic control procedures.

"The FAA will certainly want to take a closer look at this."

The controller then asked the Air France crew which departure procedure it had been instructed to follow.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Air traffic control audio captured the tense exchange as controllers worked to redirect the flights (not pictured). (iStock)

The crew later confirmed it had been assigned the SUMMR TWO departure, a published departure procedure from LAX. It was instructed to resume the route, according to the audio.

The FAA said air traffic control immediately issued corrective instructions after the Air France aircraft entered the American Airlines jet's path.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"This was a very dangerous situation and thank goodness, air traffic control was extremely proactive and turned the Air France aircraft heading west before it converged with the American Airlines flight," Arroyo said.

"The FAA will certainly want to take a closer look at this, especially since it's happened several times already here in the past years," he noted.

Arroyo said, however, that "this air traffic controller did an exceptional job."

He also pointed out that such aviation incidents are "very, very rare."

articles.title: Fire contained on platform in Iran’s South Pars gas field
articles.excerpt:
Iranian authorities have contained a fire that broke out on a platform in South Pars gas field, the world’s largest offshore natural gas field.

The Pars Oil and Gas Company said the fire broke out on...
articles.body_text:
Iranian authorities have contained a fire that broke out on a platform in South Pars gas field, the world’s largest offshore natural gas field.

The Pars Oil and Gas Company said the fire broke out on Tuesday on a gas platform in Phase 14 of the South Pars field and was extinguished immediately, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported.

“During the incident, 17 workers jumped into the sea to save their lives; rescue operations for them are currently underway,” Kourosh Dehghan, Bushehr Province’s director general of crisis management, told Fars.

“Further details regarding the scale of the incident and the condition of the workers will be announced later,” Dehghan added.

Bushehr’s crisis management office later said all 17 workers were in good condition after boarding lifeboats and rescue craft, and that three heavy rescue vessels had been sent to the platform to bring them back.

Officials are considering a gas leak or an operational mishap as possible causes for the fire, Fars said.

The news agency added that the platform accounts for only 14.5 million cubic metres of South Pars’s total daily production of more than 700 million cubic metres of gas.

Iran shares the reservoir with major gas exporter Qatar, which calls its portion the North Dome.

The reservoir contains an estimated 1,800 trillion cubic feet (51 trillion cubic metres) of usable gas, enough to supply the world’s needs for 13 years.
